vignette: Sujit, a 34-year-old chaplain of South Eastern Asian descent, has been navigating the challenges of his daily life since losing his wife two years ago. His work as a chaplain brings him comfort and solace in many ways, but it also serves as a stark reminder of the fragility of human existence. Recently, an incident has deeply shaken Sujit's sense of safety: he was mugged on his way back from a late-night vigil at a local hospice. The robbery occurred just last month on a quiet street near his home. He had left the hospital around midnight and was walking to his car when a young man, masked and armed with a knife, emerged from an alleyway. The assailant demanded that Sujit hand over his wallet and phone. In a moment of terror, Sujit complied without hesitation, but the mugger still pushed him forcefully against the wall, causing bruises on his arm and shoulder. The encounter lasted only a few minutes, yet it felt like an eternity. Since then, Sujit has struggled to shake off the pervasive feeling of unease and vulnerability that lingered long after the incident. He often finds himself hypervigilant, especially in dimly lit areas or when he's alone at night. Walking home from work now feels like a constant threat. He notices his heart rate spike whenever someone walks behind him quickly or if there are any sudden noises. At night, Sujit experiences intrusive thoughts and nightmares that replay the mugging over and over again. The vivid images of the masked figure and the cold edge of the knife against his skin cause him to wake up in a sweat, feeling as though he is reliving the event. He avoids talking about it with others, fearing that expressing his fears might further erode his sense of control. His work as a chaplain has also been affected. Sujit feels increasingly anxious when comforting families in distress, especially at night or when he's alone on duty. The constant need to be alert and ready for any threat makes it difficult for him to fully immerse himself in the spiritual support he offers. He often finds himself scanning the environment during visits, looking for potential dangers rather than focusing solely on providing emotional solace. In his personal life, Sujit has become more isolated since the mugging. He avoids going out alone at night and has even started taking taxis instead of walking to events that require him to be outdoors after dark. This change in behavior has strained his relationships with friends who don't understand why he's suddenly so wary. Sujit's attempts to cope with these overwhelming feelings include seeking comfort in prayer and meditation, but even these practices feel less soothing than they used to. He sometimes wonders if this is a sign that his faith is weakening or if it's just another symptom of the trauma he experienced. Despite these challenges, Sujit remains committed to his vocation as a chaplain. His sense of duty and compassion for others push him forward each day, even when his personal life feels chaotic and unsafe. He continues to seek solace in his faith but finds himself grappling with feelings of betrayal and loss that go beyond the immediate trauma of the mugging. The mugging has left indelible marks on Sujit's psyche, affecting not only his daily routine but also his sense of security and trust in others. As he grapples with these emotions, his work as a chaplain provides both a source of strength and an ongoing reminder of the vulnerability he now feels acutely in every aspect of his life.
